title: Abolition of slavery and the slave trade
summary: The global abolition movement dismantled legal property in human beings across empires and continents between 1787 and 1981. Driven by enslaved rebellions, mass political petitions, and civil war, it replaced transatlantic chattel slavery with international prohibitions on bondage.
card: Beginning with Quaker petitions and the 1787 formation of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in London, the anti-slavery campaign grew into a worldwide struggle shaped by enslaved revolts and constitutional politics. The Haitian Revolution established the first independent black republic through armed self-emancipation, while British legislation in 1807 and 1833 ended colonial slavery at the cost of £20 million paid to enslavers. Later milestones—including the American Civil War, Brazil's 1888 Lei Áurea, and Mauritania's 1981 decree—formally eradicated legal chattel slavery across the globe.
what:
The abolition of slavery was a protracted global movement that eliminated the legal sanction of chattel bondage across the Americas, Europe, and Africa between the late eighteenth and late twentieth centuries. Organized British campaigning coalesced on 22 May 1787, when twelve Quaker and Anglican reformers established the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in London, mobilizing public petitions, investigative pamphlets, and boycott strategies.

Enslaved people's armed resistance and self-emancipation formed the decisive engine of abolition. In Saint-Domingue, an uprising begun in August 1791 by enslaved laborers escalated into the Haitian Revolution, which defeated French expeditionary armies and culminated in Jean-Jacques Dessalines declaring Haitian independence on 1 January 1804. This victory established the modern world's first sovereign nation created by formerly enslaved people and forced European powers to reckon with the collapse of the plantation model. Frequent rebellions across the Caribbean—including the 1816 uprising in Barbados and the 1831–1832 Baptist War in Jamaica—convinced imperial administrators that slavery could no longer be sustained without catastrophic violence.

State abolition proceeded through piecemeal legislation, economic compromise, and military conflict. The British Parliament banned the slave trade in 1807 and enacted the Slavery Abolition Act in August 1833, freeing more than 800,000 enslaved people while paying £20 million in public compensation directly to slave-owners and imposing an unpaid four-year apprenticeship. In the United States, abolition required a four-year civil war and the ratification of the 13th Amendment in December 1865, which freed roughly four million individuals. Brazil enacted the Lei Áurea on 13 May 1888 without financial compensation to planters, ending legal bondage in the Western Hemisphere, while Mauritania became the last sovereign state to formally outlaw slavery by decree on 9 November 1981.

Historians disagree over whether moral activism, the economic decline of sugar monoculture, or violent slave revolt constituted the primary catalyst of abolition, but modern scholarship stresses that imperial authorities conceded emancipation only when enslaved resistance rendered the continuation of chattel slavery unmanageable.

uncertainty.note: Start date marks the founding of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in London on 22 May 1787; earlier organized initiatives include the 1783 Quaker petition to the British Parliament and the 1780 Pennsylvania gradual abolition statute. End date is 9 November 1981, when Mauritania passed Decree 81-234, the last country to formally abolish slavery by statutory decree.

how: Abolition operated through interlocking legal, economic, and military mechanisms across multiple continents. First, transatlantic networks of African and European reformers gathered empirical testimony, circulated pamphlets such as Olaudah Equiano's autobiography, and mobilized hundreds of thousands of signatures on legislative petitions. Second, enslaved populations engaged in continuous sabotage, marronage, and large-scale insurrections that escalated the military and financial costs of colonial policing to intolerable levels. Third, imperial and national legislatures enacted statutory prohibitions, beginning with bans on slave trading in Britain and the United States in 1807–1808, followed by emancipatory legislation. In Britain, parliamentary passage was brokered through a £20 million treasury payout to enslavers and a coercive apprenticeship system. In the United States, secession and military necessity led to Abraham Lincoln's 1863 Emancipation Proclamation and the constitutional prohibition of slavery under the 13th Amendment. In Brazil, urban mobilization and mass desertions from coffee estates forced imperial sanction of the Lei Áurea in 1888, while international human rights pressure ultimately compelled postcolonial states like Mauritania to declare legal abolition in 1981.
why_it_matters:
The abolition of slavery fundamentally transformed global jurisprudence, economics, and human rights by invalidating the legal claim of property in human beings. It dismantled the economic foundations of transatlantic plantation capitalism, freeing tens of millions of enslaved people over two centuries and establishing the core legal principle of universal bodily freedom that later anchored the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights. However, emancipation was structurally compromised: European and American governments prioritized the property claims of enslavers through massive financial indemnities, while former slaves received neither land nor reparations, entrenching enduring racialized poverty, sharecropping, and vagrancy laws.

Had enslaved workers not rebelled in Saint-Domingue and across the Caribbean, European empires might have expanded plantation slavery well into the twentieth century, relying on intensified mechanization and brutal coercion rather than conceding emancipation. Without the 13th Amendment and the defeat of the Confederacy, North America would have remained fractured by an aggressive slaveholding oligarchy, drastically altering the industrial and geopolitical trajectory of the Atlantic world. Even today, the financial legacies of enslaver compensation and the persistence of descent-based servitude in regions like the Sahel demonstrate that the global struggle for genuine emancipation remains an unfinished historic process.

perspectives.account: Williams argued that the abolition of the British slave trade and slavery was driven primarily by economic calculation rather than moral philanthropy: the decline of West Indian sugar profitability, soil depletion, and the rise of industrial capitalism, which demanded free-trade markets and wage labor rather than mercantilist colonial monopolies.

perspectives.holder: Humanitarian and evangelical interpretation (Reginald Coupland, traditional British historiography)
perspectives.account: This traditional school viewed British abolition as an unselfish moral crusade and a triumph of Christian philanthropy, crediting parliamentary reformers, evangelical leaders such as William Wilberforce, and public anti-slavery petitions with overcoming vested colonial economic interests.

perspectives.holder: Self-emancipation and black agency perspective (C.L.R. James, Robin Blackburn, and modern social historians)
perspectives.account: Emphasizes that enslaved people themselves were the primary agents of their liberation. The armed triumph of the Haitian Revolution and recurrent plantation rebellions (including Barbados in 1816, Demerara in 1823, and Jamaica's 1831–1832 Baptist War) rendered chattel slavery politically and militarily untenable, forcing metropolitan governments to legislate abolition to prevent catastrophic imperial defeat.

perspectives.holder: Enslaver compensation and capital continuity perspective (UCL Legacies of British Slavery; Bank of England study)
perspectives.account: Demonstrates that the 1833 British abolition settlement was a massive state-funded financial rescue of slave-owners, distributing £20 million across roughly 40,000 compensation claims while compelling freed people into years of uncompensated apprenticeship, cementing wealth inequality and racial hierarchies across modern financial and imperial institutions.

numbers.label: British government compensation paid to slave-owners under the 1833 Act
numbers.note: Statutory compensation sum of twenty million pounds agreed by the British government to compensate slave-owners for the loss of claimed property; formerly enslaved people received no compensation.

numbers.label: Enslaved Africans emancipated in British colonies under the 1833 Act
numbers.note: Estimated count of more than 800,000 enslaved Africans in the British colonies emancipated by the 1833 legislation, initially subjected to compulsory apprenticeship.

numbers.note: Negative roll-call votes in the US House of Representatives on 31 January 1865 (the measure passed 119 to 56).
